analysis.one_liner: Blocks insurers from denying free COVID-19 testing and exposes providers charging inflated test prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was assigned to and died when the Congress ended, so no protections became law.
analysis.plain_summary: During the pandemic, federal law already required insurers to cover COVID-19 tests for free, but some people still got surprise bills. This bill would have stopped insurers from second-guessing why someone got tested, whether they had symptoms, or how often they tested as a way to deny the free coverage. It also would have required the government to survey hundreds of providers' cash prices for tests, publish a report comparing them, and name providers charging extreme prices. The bill was sent to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who sought COVID-19 tests would be protected from insurers rejecting their free-coverage claim based on why they got tested, whether they showed symptoms, or how often they tested. Patients would also get clearer guidance about billing, and providers would be told not to collect out-of-pocket charges. The public would gain access to a government report showing average cash prices for tests, which providers were charging them, and which providers' prices were far above the norm.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines 'medical management' to include determinations about why a person sought testing, whether they showed symptoms, what provider ordered the test, and how often they tested — and under existing law, insurers cannot use medical management to deny free COVID-19 test coverage, so this closes a route around that guarantee.
It lets insurers still encourage people to use lower-priced testing sites, as long as those efforts do not delay or block access to testing.

It directs HHS to survey at least 200 providers of different sizes and locations on their published cash prices for COVID-19 testing and related services, then publish a report showing compliance rates, average cash prices, comparisons to Medicare rates, and the names of providers charging outlier prices that far exceed the average.

It requires HHS, Labor, and Treasury to jointly issue guidance clarifying the claims process so people are not hit with cost-sharing or prior authorization, and telling providers not to collect cost-sharing from patients seeking COVID-19 testing.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose a way to scrutinize and potentially deny testing claims. Testing providers that charge unusually high cash prices — including some hospitals and freestanding emergency rooms — would be named in a public federal report, creating reputational and market pressure. Providers generally would face clearer federal instructions not to bill patients directly for tests.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it addresses surprise bills for COVID-19 testing only, not the much broader problem of surprise bills for emergency and out-of-network care generally.

Its main enforcement tools are paperwork — a survey, a public report, and guidance — rather than penalties, so a provider that ignored the cash-price publishing requirement or charged extreme prices would face public naming but no fine.
A good-faith objection: defining 'medical management' so broadly could make it harder for insurers to police wasteful or duplicate testing, raising coverage costs that flow into premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real but modest. The strongest part is plugging a loophole that let insurers deny free testing based on a patient's symptoms or reasons for testing, which mattered most early in the pandemic when testing access was critical. The transparency provisions name high-priced providers but impose no financial penalty, and the whole bill does nothing about surprise bills beyond COVID testing. Its cost to insurers and a subset of providers is small; the benefit to patients would have been meaningful but limited to one category of care.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the bill on September 29, 2020, with five Democratic cosponsors, in the final months of the 116th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.
The bill was written to tighten the existing requirement that insurers cover COVID-19 diagnostic testing at no cost, without prior authorization or other medical management.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who received surprise bills for COVID-19 tests got no federal fix. Health insurers kept the ability to scrutinize testing claims, and providers charging high cash prices for tests avoided being publicly named in a federal report.

for.name: Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block surprise bills for COVID-19 testing.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, but no vote was ever taken and no senator publicly opposed the bill, so the partisan shape of the outcome cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would bar insurers from using review of a patient's symptoms, testing frequency, or reasons for testing to deny free COVID-19 test coverage. That closes a cost-control route that shifted testing bills onto patients.

industries.industry: Hospitals, laboratories, and freestanding emergency rooms charging high cash test prices
industries.note: A federal survey and report would name providers whose cash prices for COVID-19 testing substantially exceeded the average, exposing them to public pressure. The bill imposes no fines, only transparency.

industries.industry: Insurers' group health plan customers and employers
industries.note: Joint federal guidance would clarify claims submission so patients are not charged cost-sharing and providers are told not to bill them, while still allowing plans to steer patients to cheaper test sites.
